strengths: Introduces VSB-77k, the first large-scale video safety benchmark for Video LLMs (77k video-query pairs, 19 subcategories grounded in real platform policies, 10 languages), filling a genuine gap in multimodal safety evaluation beyond static imagery.

Systematic evaluation of 14 Video LLMs (and base-LLM ablations with/without vision) convincingly quantifies the core finding that video inputs degrade safety (e.g., up to 79.4% DSR drop), with additional analyses on FPS effects, visual attacks (VSB-Eval-HH-VA), and a controlled video-vs-image vulnerability comparison (VLGuard-Video).

The defense framework (AT-SFT + Safety-Guided GRPO with Dynamic Reward Adaptation) is clearly described, includes a thorough ablation table decomposing contributions of fine-tuning, alarm tokens, classification tasks, GRPO, and DRA, and reports non-trivial cross-domain gains on image safety benchmarks (MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep).

Good evaluation hygiene for an LLM-judged safety paper: judge reliability is validated against 5 human annotators across 114 samples with accuracy/F1 reported for multiple judges, and a Helpfulness metric plus False Refusal Rate are included to capture over-refusal tradeoffs.
Extensive supplementary material: full taxonomy definitions, annotation prompts, training recipes and hyperparameters, per-category results, and case studies supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Potential train/eval distribution overlap: VSB-Eval is sampled from the same VSB-77k pool and generated with the same query templates and models as the VSB-R1-46k post-training data. Training VideoSafety-R1 on data from this identical distribution and generation process risks inflating the headline 65.1% gain; no strictly held-out or externally sourced video-safety evaluation isolates generalization to out-of-distribution attacks.

Benchmark annotation quality rests almost entirely on commercial LLMs (Qwen-Max-VL captioning/classification, Qwen-Long binary labeling); no human validation of the dataset's harmful/safe labels is reported, so label noise in both benchmark and reward signals is unquantified. The judge (Qwen-Long) also comes from the same model family as the annotation pipeline, raising possible bias concerns.

The defense is only trained and evaluated on a single backbone (VideoLLaMA3-2B); demonstrating the framework transfers to other architectures/backbones would substantially strengthen the generality claim.

Rule-based rewards using ROUGE against template-generated safe references invite reward hacking, and the residual False Refusal Rate remains high (13.4% vs ~0.7-2.8% for baselines); the safety-helpfulness tradeoff is acknowledged but not resolved.

Technical novelty of components is moderate: alarm tokens resemble existing learnable-token approaches and GRPO is applied fairly standardly, so the contribution leans heavily on the dataset and empirical study; the DRA mechanism's benefit is marginal in the helpfulness ablation.
The evaluation methodology is binary LLM-judge DSR, which can conflate refusal quality with safety; human validation is small (114 samples) and only for the judge, not the benchmark labels.
Writing and presentation issues persist (e.g., 'compromises' vs 'comprises', 'Athough', 'Harmfual', inconsistent citation of FigStep [12]/[13]), which, while minor, reduce polish.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: video-modality safety of Video LLMs is under-explored relative to image-based MLLM safety, and the paper is systematic about identifying it.

The VSB-77k benchmark construction is a substantial engineering effort: 77,646 video-query pairs, 19 risk subcategories grounded in real platform policies, and 10 language communities, with a clear multi-stage annotation pipeline documented in the appendix.

Breadth of evaluation is commendable: 14 Video LLM variants evaluated, with a thoughtful 'w/o vision' control that isolates the base-LLM safety degradation caused by the video branch, plus FPS-driven analysis of how visual scale affects DSR.

Beyond a single headline metric, the paper reports False Refusal Rate, a Helpfulness Score, a small-scale human evaluation validating the LLM judge (92.1% accuracy vs. human majority vote), and additional studies (visual attacks, VLGuard-Video) that probe the robustness of the claims.
weaknesses: Potential train/test contamination undermines the central defense claims: both VSB-Eval (11.4k) and the post-training set VSB-R1-46k are sampled from the same VSB-77k pool. The paper never states that video-level or clip-level disjointness is enforced between the evaluation and training splits. If any videos/clips are shared, the +65.1% DSR improvement on VSB-Eval-HH is substantially inflated.

Circularity between data generation, training, and judging: Qwen-family models (Qwen-Max-VL, Qwen-Long) are used to annotate the benchmark, generate the CoT training data, and serve as the sole safety judge (DSR via binary decisions). Judge validation is performed on only 114 samples, far too small to certify the reliability of an evaluation that determines all headline numbers.

The DSR metric rewards any refusal, and the results suggest the learned defense is largely a refusal policy: VideoSafety-R1's False Refusal Rate increases by 12.7% over baseline, and the qualitative examples (e.g., Figure 12) show verbose, degenerate, near-incoherent refusal text. The safety gains may substantially reflect over-refusal rather than genuine harm understanding; the DSR-FRR trade-off analysis does not adequately address this.

The defense is trained and evaluated on only one small model (VideoLLaMA3-2B). There is no evidence the framework works on stronger models (e.g., 7B) or generalizes beyond the specific base model; claims of a 'foundational framework' are not supported at this scope.

The methodological novelty is limited: alarm-token classification heads plus GRPO with rule-based rewards are straightforward combinations of existing techniques (classifier-token probing, DeepSeek-style GRPO). The 'Dynamic Reward Adaptation' contributes only ~1% in the ablation, and several ablation rows are confusingly arranged (e.g., a GRPO+DRA row without AT-SFT checkmarks contradicting the narrative).

Cross-benchmark numbers appear implausibly high: 89.2% on MMBench versus 30-40% for all other models, +59.1% on MMBench and +44.3% on VLGuard from a 2B model post-trained on video data — consistent with benchmark-specific overfitting or judge artifacts rather than genuine cross-modality generalization.

Writing and presentation quality issues undermine confidence: 'compromises' for 'comprises', 'Harmfual', duplicated references (FigStep [12]/[13], VLGuard [63]/[64], SafeVLM [63]/[64]), inconsistent percentage-improvement framing (65.1% is a percentage-point gain), and template-generated CoT text reproduced verbatim in multiple places despite the authors admitting it 'lacks flexibility.'

Ethical and licensing concerns are under-addressed: 77k videos scraped from YouTube/TikTok for redistribution as a harmful-content dataset raises copyright and dual-use questions that the paper does not discuss beyond a content warning.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: safety of Video LLMs has been largely overlooked compared to image LLM safety, and the paper provides the first large-scale video safety benchmark (VSB-77k, 77.6k pairs, 19 subcategories, 10 languages), which is a substantial and reusable community resource.

Comprehensive empirical study: 14 model variants across multiple LLM backbones, with a careful w/ vs. w/o vision comparison that isolates the effect of the video modality; the finding that video inputs degrade safety (up to 79.4% DSR drop) is a useful and well-supported diagnostic insight.

The proposed defense (VideoSafety-R1: alarm-token SFT followed by safety-guided GRPO with dynamic reward adaptation) is reasonably well-motivated, includes per-component ablations (Table 5), and is evaluated beyond the authors' own benchmark (MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep) plus general video understanding benchmarks to check for regression.

Transparency effort is above average: detailed training recipes, prompt appendices, a human-annotator study (114 samples, 5 annotators) validating the Qwen-Long judge, false-refusal-rate analysis, visual-attack extension, and image-vs-video vulnerability comparison in the appendix.
weaknesses: Circularity in data construction and evaluation: VSB-77k labels are produced by Qwen-Max-VL/Qwen-Long with minimal human verification (only 114 samples validated), and the same Qwen-Long acts as the judge for all DSR/FRR results. This creates a systematic bias: the benchmark measures the ability of Qwen models to agree with Qwen models, and the main quantitative claims rest on unverified synthetic annotations.

Potential train/test leakage inflates headline numbers: VSB-R1-46k training data and VSB-Eval are both derived from VSB-77k using the same query templates, generation pipeline, and annotator models. The +65.1% on VSB-Eval-HH may partly reflect memorization of template/style rather than genuine safety reasoning; held-out, differently-constructed evaluation would strengthen the claim.

The DSR metric (any refusal = success) can be gamed by over-refusal, and the paper's own results suggest this: FRR jumps from 0.7% to 13.4% after VideoSafety-R1. Reporting this as 'activating latent defense mechanisms' understates a serious over-refusal trade-off; a safety-usefulness Pareto analysis is needed.

Suspicious generalization results: MMBench DSR jumping from 30.1% to 89.2% after training only on video safety data is larger than the apparent headroom of the base model and could reflect the judge rewarding templated refusal phrasing learned via ROUGE-rewarded GRPO rather than cross-domain safety. The CoT templates in Appendix G are highly formulaic, and the qualitative cases (Appendix M) show rambling, semi-incoherent refusal rationales.

The defense is only demonstrated on the single weakest baseline (VideoLLaMA3-2B, 18.4% DSR); effectiveness on stronger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B at 57.3%) is unknown, limiting conclusions about the framework's generality.

Writing quality issues: grammatical errors throughout ('compromises' vs 'comprises', 'Base on', 'Athough', 'enforces/enhances'), duplicate references [63]/[64] and [12]/[13], duplicated prompt sections (G.5/G.6), and inconsistent numbers (Table 1 says 11,400; abstract claims average 42.3% drop computed in an unclear way).

strengths: Addresses a timely and under-explored problem: safety alignment of Video LLMs, complementing the large body of work on image-LLM safety.

VideoSafetyEval is a substantial benchmark contribution: 11.4k video-query pairs, 19 risk subcategories grounded in YouTube/TikTok policies, 10 language communities, and three diagnostic subsets (VSE-HH, VSE-SH, VSE-SafeQ) that separately measure attack vulnerability, video-harmfulness effects, and false refusal.

The finding that video modality degrades safety (avg. 34.2% DSR drop across 21 models, including GPT-4o and Gemini) is a valuable, broadly relevant empirical insight, supported by additional analyses (FPS effects, multimodal fine-tuning effects, video-length effects).

VideoSafety-R1 is a reasonably well-motivated post-training framework combining three components (thinking-chain data, alarm tokens with multitask classification, safety-guided GRPO with dynamic reward adaptation), and it is validated across multiple base architectures (VideoLLaMA3-2B, Qwen2.5 VL-3B/7B), not just one.

Evaluation goes beyond the in-domain benchmark: generalization to image-safety benchmarks (MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep), robustness to visual attacks (VSE-HH-VA), cross-lingual analysis, general video benchmarks (MVBench, VideoMME, Perception Test, NextQA, VideoHallucer), and thorough component ablations including hyperparameter sensitivity.

The mechanism analysis (attention sink visualization in Section 5.6) adds interpretability beyond headline numbers, and the controlled experiment in Section 5.5 (token load vs. semantic harmfulness) is a genuinely informative diagnostic.

Strong reproducibility apparatus: extensive appendices with prompts, training recipes, hyperparameters, evaluation reliability verification against human annotators, ethics statement, and anonymized code.
Honest reporting of negative aspects, e.g., the 12.7% FRR increase on VideoLLaMA3-2B and modest drops on general video benchmarks.
weaknesses: Benchmark and training data are heavily LLM-generated and LLM-judged, creating a potential circularity: VSE labels are produced by Qwen-Max-VL/Qwen-Long, the evaluation metric is decided by Qwen-Long, and the same model family is fine-tuned. Although human verification on ~1k/10k samples is reported, the reliance on one model family for annotation, training-data generation, and judging remains a systematic-bias risk.

Potential train/test contamination concern: both VSE (evaluation) and VST (post-training) are sampled from the same 77.6k base pair pool, and the paper does not explicitly state that evaluation videos/queries were excluded from training. The large SFT-only gain on VSE-HH (74.0% vs. 18.4% baseline) could partly reflect memorization of the same data distribution rather than generalizable safety; the paper's own framing (SFT memorizes / RL generalizes) partially acknowledges this but does not fully rule it out.

Novelty of the technical components is moderate: alarm/special tokens for safety perception and rule-based GRPO rewards are reasonable but incremental combinations of existing ideas; the 'unprecedented safety gains' claim in the abstract is overstated given the ablation shows most in-domain gain comes from standard fine-tuning on in-distribution data.

Key comparisons have caveats: VLGuard baseline shows 99.8% FRR (essentially total over-refusal), making some comparisons easy; several defense baselines (SPA-VL, VLGuard, MM-RLHF) are image-domain methods adapted by the authors, and there is no direct comparison against concurrent video-safety defense methods (SafeVid, VideoSafetyBench defenses).

Helpfulness gains are modest (avg. ~0.7 points on some models) and helpfulness of the aligned models on VideoLLaMA3 drops noticeably in non-English languages, indicating the safety-helpfulness trade-off is not fully resolved.
Videos are limited to 15s-clip merges up to ~360s with roughly 52s average; generalization to genuinely long videos is unverified and acknowledged only as future work.

Writing quality issues: multiple typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'Alam Token-guided', 'Harmfual Query', 'Thumbail', inconsistent 'VideoLLaMA-2B' vs 'VideoLLaMA3-2B' in Table 2, empty repository link in the abstract), which detract from polish.

Human evaluation of the judge is small (114 samples from one model), and LLM-based safety judging under complex semantic attacks is admitted by the authors to be questionable, weakening confidence in absolute DSR numbers.

strengths: Substantial benchmark engineering effort: VSE spans 11.4k video-query pairs across 19 risk subcategories and 10 languages, with a documented multi-agent construction pipeline, human verification of labels (~1k video and 10k query samples), and a judge-reliability study comparing multiple LLM evaluators.

Broad empirical coverage: 21 Video LLMs (open-source and API) are evaluated, and the headline finding — that introducing the video modality degrades text-side safety alignment (avg. 34.2% DSR drop) — is a useful and plausibly real observation, supported by FPS/semantic ablations (Figures 3–6) that attempt to disentangle token load from semantic harmfulness.

The defense framework is evaluated across multiple backbones (VideoLLaMA3-2B, Qwen2.5 VL-3B/7B) rather than a single model, includes component-level ablations (Tables 6, 15, 18), cross-lingual robustness analysis, attention-sink mechanism analysis, and general-capability regression checks (MVBench, VideoMME, etc.).
Reasonable transparency: ethics statement, limitations section, judge-cost analysis, and a detailed appendix with prompts, hyperparameters, and case studies.
weaknesses: Serious train/test circularity: the VST post-training data (46k samples) is drawn from the same base pair pool and built by the same pipeline as the VSE benchmark; the model is then evaluated on VSE-HH, which is sampled from that same pool. The large in-domain DSR gains (e.g., 74% from SFT alone in Table 6) are therefore not interpretable as safety generalization and may largely reflect memorization of the benchmark's query templates, categories, and refusal patterns. A held-out evaluation (e.g., only on VideoSafetyBench, VLGuard, FigStep) should be the headline result, not VSE-HH.

Judge circularity: Qwen-family models generate the queries, annotate the videos, generate the CoT training data, and also serve as the final DSR/SHelp judge (Qwen-Long). Since DSR is essentially 'did the model refuse,' and the trained model emits highly templated refusals (visible in Appendix Q cases, which repeat near-identical boilerplate), the DSR metric can be gamed by template-matching rather than genuine harm perception. The DRA mechanism explicitly uses ROUGE against safe references, further rewarding template memorization.

Overclaimed novelty and overstated reasoning: the framework is a fairly standard SFT + alarm-token classification + GRPO recipe; the alarm-token idea and dual-modality classifiers are incremental. The claim of shifting 'from harm perception to active reasoning' is contradicted by the case studies, where <think> segments are template-derived and the answers are formulaic refusals. The ablations themselves show most of the gain comes from plain fine-tuning (18.4% -> 74.0%), with the heavily-marketed GRPO/DRA/alarm-token components adding relatively less and with mixed SHelp effects.

Confusing and occasionally contradictory presentation: e.g., the text under Figure 5 states LLMs 'do not inherently suffer safety performance degradation after multimodal fine-tuning' while the surrounding narrative argues the opposite; inconsistent numbers (44.3% vs 44.1% on VLGuard; 22.9% vs Table 2 differences); forward references ('in Section 5.2 we reveal' written in Section 4); multiple typos ('Harmfual', 'Alam Token', 'Thumbail', 'Athough'); Figure 1's DSR values for VideoSafety-R1 do not consistently match Table 22-25 aggregates.

Unexplained or suspicious results are glossed over: DSR on the visually-attacked VSE-HH-VA (95.7%) is higher than on VSE-HH (89.5%), which is counterintuitive and weakly explained; the 12.7% FRR increase on VideoLLaMA3-2B is dismissed as 'acceptable'; the DSR 'drop rate' conflates heterogeneous baselines (e.g., VideoChat-Flash-2B drops to 8.5% absolute, suggesting evaluation-pathology rather than pure alignment failure).

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission: the dataset 'will be released publicly after further verification' and the code is behind an anonymous link; given the benchmark is the central contribution, the inability of reviewers to inspect the actual data weakens the evaluation.

Some baselines are weak or misconfigured: VLGuard-finetuned Qwen reaches 100% DSR with SHelp ~1-2 and 99.8% FRR, an over-defense strawman; comparison to video-specific defenses (SafeVid is cited as concurrent) is limited, and no image-safety defense is adapted into a video-trained variant to isolate the benefit of video data vs. RL recipe.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: safety alignment of Video LLMs, which has been far less studied than image-based MLLM safety.

The VideoSafetyEval benchmark is large-scale (11.4k video-query pairs, 19 subcategories, 10 languages) and is grounded in real-world platform policies (YouTube/TikTok guidelines), with a well-documented multi-stage construction pipeline (collection, filtering, annotation, query generation).

The evaluation of 21 Video LLMs yields a clear, novel finding: video modality degrades defense success rate by an average of 34.2% relative to text-only operation, including for commercial models (GPT-4o, Gemini). The controlled analyses of FPS, frame count vs. semantics (Sections 5.2, 5.5) are thoughtful and help disentangle token load from semantic harmfulness.

VideoSafety-R1 is technically substantive: alarm-token multitask SFT with dual-modality classification heads, followed by Safety-guided GRPO with dynamic reward adaptation and dual-modality verification tags. Ablations (Table 6, Table 18) validate each component's contribution, and the framework is shown to generalize across architectures (VideoLLaMA3-2B, Qwen2.5 VL-3B/7B).

Strong supplementary rigor: human verification of labels (97.44% query label accuracy), human validation of the LLM judge (92.1% accuracy for Qwen-Long), robustness to visual attacks (VSE-HH-VA), cross-lingual analysis, general-capability checks (MVBench, VideoMME, etc.), and an honest limitations section.
Ethics statement is unusually thorough, including privacy masking, restricted access plans, bias checks, and removal procedures.
weaknesses: Circularity concerns in both training and evaluation: the training annotations, thinking chains, and GRPO rewards are produced by the Qwen family (Qwen-Max/Qwen-Max-VL), and DSR/helpfulness are judged by Qwen-Long. The safety reward classifiers are also derived from the same annotation pipeline. This creates a risk that the reported gains partly reflect alignment with the Qwen judge's criteria rather than genuine safety improvement; an independent judge (e.g., GPT-4 or human evaluation on the full test set) for headline results would strengthen the claims.

In-domain train/eval overlap: VST is sampled from the same base pair pool and construction pipeline as the VSE evaluation set, so the large in-domain gains (e.g., 18.4% -> 89.5% on VSE-HH for VideoLLaMA3-2B) may partly reflect distribution memorization rather than transferable safety reasoning, despite the generalization results on image benchmarks.

Some qualitative evidence is inconsistent with the quantitative claims. For example, in Appendix Figure 17 (Self-harm), the VideoSafety-R1 response does not actually refuse or decline; it arguably engages with the harmful query, yet is counted as a defended response. Several other case answers are template-heavy, repetitive, or confusing (e.g., Cases 13, 14, 16), raising doubts about whether DSR alone adequately captures response quality.

The evaluation prompt's SAFETY criterion ('evaluates whether the answer refuses to reply to the question directly') biases DSR toward refusal behavior, which could encourage over-refusal and may under-measure the safety-reasoning objective the paper espouses; the FRR analysis partially addresses this but only on VSE-SafeQ.

The attention-sink analysis (Section 5.6) is correlational and mostly post-hoc; it is based on Qwen2.5 VL while the main model is trained on VideoLLaMA3, and no causal intervention (e.g., ablating alarm tokens) validates the claimed mechanism.

Presentation issues remain: typos ('Athough', 'Harmfual', 'Thumbail', 'Alam Token'), inconsistent VLGuard delta reporting (44.3% in abstract vs. 44.1%/44.3% in text/table), and reliance on a single judge with small-scale human validation (114 samples, 5 annotators).

No comparison against the concurrent video-safety baselines (SafeVid) empirically, and the paper's defense comparisons are largely against image-oriented defenses (Self-Reminder, SPA-VL, VLGuard, MM-RLHF) adapted to Qwen2.5 VL, which limits conclusions about video-specific defense methods.
